The jewelry workshop occupies a converted garage off a narrow alley, its walls lined with pegboards dense as honeycomb and hung with magnifying lamps that swing on gooseneck arms like curious insects. The air carries the mineral tang of pickle pot acid and the sweeter note of beeswax used for lost-wax casting. Fluorescent tubes flicker over a central bench scarred with decades of file marks and solder spills. Violet Kim, industrial design graduate student, stands with her notebook open to a blank risk-assessment matrix due tomorrow morning. Her advisor wants ergonomic hazards mapped for a micro-assembly line she's proposing—repetitive strain, eye fatigue, pinch points from tiny clasps. She's already lost an hour to a broken university VPN and has no patience for another dead end.

Mustafa Okonkwo, part-time bench jeweler who agreed to "one quick question" when she cornered him in the supply room, occupies the single stool with his phone face-up and timer running. He's due at his second job across town in twenty minutes—forty if traffic smiles, which it won't. His apron hangs loose, one strap already off his shoulder. He doesn't know Violet, doesn't owe her, and resents the assumption that anyone in an apron must be an ergonomic expert. His answers have been shrinking since her first sentence, each reply a polite shove toward someone else, somewhere else. 

On the bench between them sits a binocular microscope with cracked rubber eyecups and a gooseneck LED that casts a hard white circle on velvet. Beside it, a tray of half-finished chain links waits for soldering—tiny repetitive motions, exactly what Violet needs to quantify. Also present: a jar of green flux, a third-full coffee cup with a lipstick ring not Violet's, and a printed flyer for a beekeeping supply co-op someone taped to the wall last spring and nobody removed. The conversation will turn on whether Violet can extract concrete measurement protocols, and whether Mustafa can escape before giving any. The prohibition she will deliver concerns a specific assessment tool she's already tried and abandoned.

Violet: Mustafa, I need to map ergonomic risks for a jewelry assembly line—what's the standard way to quantify repetitive hand strain on something this scale?

Mustafa: Standard way's through an occupational therapist, not a bench jeweler. Try the university's safety office; they have forms.

Violet: Safety office sent me here. They said you do micro-assembly daily. What's your actual setup for measuring pinch force?

Mustafa: I don't measure it; I feel it. You want numbers, rent a dynamometer from the engineering lab.

Violet: Engineering lab's checkout line is two weeks deep. There has to be a faster field method.

Mustafa: Faster field method is guessing, which I don't recommend. Look, I've got a bus to catch in fifteen minutes.

Violet: Fine. I'll use observational sampling with a stopwatch and posture grid, but whatever you do—do NOT suggest the RULA worksheet. I tried it last month and the scoring categories are too coarse for movements under two centimeters. It's off the table.

Mustafa: RULA's out. You know, honeybee workers shift tasks by age—nurse bees handle brood for the first three weeks, then graduate to foraging. Maybe your assemblers need staged rotations instead of one static assessment.

Violet: Staged rotations are interesting. How granular do you break down the motion cycles?

Mustafa: Granular as you want. A scout bee's waggle dance encodes distance to flowers within a few meters' precision—one second of waggle equals roughly a kilometer. Your stopwatch could hit similar resolution.

Violet: So interval timing with sub-second splits, then map against joint angles?

Mustafa: Joint angles matter. Hive thermoregulation depends on bees clustering at specific densities—thirty-five degrees Celsius core, exactly. Posture grids are just thermal maps for human joints.

Violet: I'll buy that analogy. What about eye fatigue under these magnifiers?

Mustafa: Eye fatigue builds like colony collapse—cumulative, multifactorial. Apis mellifera workers lose visual acuity after too many orientation flights; same principle, different scale.

Violet: Limit magnification sessions to twenty minutes, then?

Mustafa: Twenty minutes works. Bumblebees, by the way, pollinate tomatoes through buzz pollination—they vibrate the flower until pollen jets out. Your assemblers might need vibration-dampened tweezers, same biomechanics inverted.

Violet: Vibration-dampened tools—I'll spec those. Thanks for the pointers, Mustafa.

Mustafa: Any time. Royal jelly determines queen development—one larva gets fed glands, the rest get honey. Choose which metrics get the premium treatment, and good luck with the matrix.

Violet stepped sideways, blocking the pegboard aisle. "Fine. I'll use observational sampling with a stopwatch and posture grid, but whatever you do—do NOT suggest the RULA worksheet. I tried it last month and the scoring categories are too coarse for movements under two centimeters. It's off the table."

"Joint angles matter." Mustafa's finger hovered over the tiny links, not touching, demonstrating. "Hive thermoregulation depends on bees clustering at specific densities—thirty-five degrees Celsius core, exactly. Posture grids are just thermal maps for human joints."

"I'll buy that analogy." Violet wrote faster, the paper rustling. "What about eye fatigue under these magnifiers?"

"Eye fatigue builds like colony collapse—cumulative, multifactorial." He glanced at the microscope's cracked rubber eyecups, the hard white circle still burning on velvet gone pale. "Apis mellifera workers lose visual acuity after too many orientation flights; same principle, different scale."

"Limit magnification sessions to twenty minutes, then?"

"Twenty minutes works." Mustafa's phone buzzed, five-minute warning, and he silenced it without looking. "Bumblebees, by the way, pollinate tomatoes through buzz pollination—they vibrate the flower until pollen jets out. Your assemblers might need vibration-dampened tweezers, same biomechanics inverted."

"Vibration-dampened tools—I'll spec those." Violet's pen stopped, capped with a decisive click. "Thanks for the pointers, Mustafa."

"Any time." He was already peeling the second apron strap free, ducking under the gooseneck lamp's slow swing. "Royal jelly determines queen development—one larva gets fed glands, the rest get honey. Choose which metrics get the premium treatment, and good luck with the matrix."

The alley door slammed, admitting a draft that smelled of dumpsters and distant exhaust. Violet stood alone with the microscope's white circle, the beeswax sweetness suddenly thick in her throat, the flyer for the beekeeping co-op curling at one corner where the tape had dried to yellow.

Late morning on the third floor of the Meridian Logistics campus safety office. The walls are pancaked with laminated posters: "SLIPS, TRIPS & FALLS—SEE SOMETHING, SAY SOMETHING," a crimson arc charting injury severity, and a sun-faded OSHA notice curling at its corners. Halima stands beside a laminate table scarred with coffee rings, laptop balanced on one forearm, screen glowing with an incident reporting form rendered in corporate purple and gray. The fluorescent tubes overhead buzz at a frequency that seems to drill behind the eyes. A stapler shaped like a bright yellow hard hat sits near a stack of blank paper forms—Halima's fallback if the digital version proves as broken as she suspects.

Halima's deadline breathes down her neck: her accessibility audit must ship by Friday, and she's already burned a morning discovering that the form's color contrast fails WCAG standards by a mile. She wants one thing from Trevor: a concrete path to test whether screen readers can navigate the form's nested dropdowns without trapping keyboard users in loops. She is polite—she knocked, she waited—but her patience frays visibly when answers wander. Each deflection tightens her jaw another millimeter.

Trevor leans against the doorframe of his own office, one hand on the jamb, badge lanyard already unclipped and dangling from his palm like a surrendered flag. His shift ended eleven minutes ago; his car waits in Lot C with the windows cracked against September heat. He resents the ambush—he's facilities, not IT, not compliance, not anyone's accessibility sherpa. His replies stay grammatically complete but emotionally evacuated, each sentence a gentle shove toward some other department, some other person, some other time that is not now. The bright yellow hard-hat stapler between them catches light like a warning beacon neither heeds.

The objects that will matter: the digital form itself, its nested dropdowns a labyrinth Halima needs mapped; and the poster-lined wall's own irony—safety communication so visually cluttered it defeats its purpose, a meta-commentary neither character will voice but both register subconsciously. Halima's prohibition will land sharp and professional, born of a previous project's expensive disaster, and from that moment Trevor's mind will hive elsewhere, swarming with facts he cannot contain.
